item.title: France protests for fifth Saturday against living costs and heavy-handed policing
item.description: Different causes are set to come together for one march in Paris this Saturday. Campaign groups, students and Yellow Vest protesters are due to join forces in the capital, bringing together demands on wages, education and civil liberties. But after weeks of demonstrations, union leaders warn that protest fatigue is setting in, while police officers are seeking better compensation for the risk of policing the protests. Story by Jack Pownall. Fuente: France 24 - English.
item.dc:creator: FRANCE24

item.title: How Chinese custom ‘chong xi,’ or ‘clashing with joy,’ can counteract misfortune
item.description: In ancient China, when a man became seriously ill, his family might arrange a wedding for him in an attempt to drive away the disease. The custom is called chong xi, literally translated as “clashing with joy”. Its rationale is that a happy event could lift one’s spirits and thereby dispel illness or other misfortunes. In practice, if a man who was already engaged became seriously ill, his family might move his wedding forward. If he did not yet have a fiancée, his family might hastily find him... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Alice Yan

item.title: Wearing briefs boosts erectile dysfunction risk, 26,000-man study in China finds
item.description: From A-list underwear campaigns to everyday wardrobe staples, tight briefs are often hailed as the ultimate symbol of masculine appeal. However, a major new study out of China suggests that choosing tight underwear over classic boxer shorts could lead to higher rates of erectile dysfunction, premature ejaculation and prostatitis. A snug fit also impairs sperm quality, according to the findings published in the Asian Journal of Andrology last month. Loose underwear may offer a simple alternative... Fuente: South China Morning Post.

item.title: Crossing Afghanistan along the 'highway of death'
item.description: Highway 1, or the Ring Road, connects Afghanistan's major cities. After September 11, 2001, it became a hotspot for crime and fighting, particularly between the capital Kabul and Kandahar, the Taliban's birthplace. People taking it had to navigate extortions, kidnappings and suicide bombings. What has become of the road after the US-led war and five years of Taliban rule? Our former Afghanistan correspondent Claire Billet and photojournalist Sandra Calligaro returned to the country to find out. Fuente: France 24 - English.
